classical nanomedicinal carrier materials do not significantly improve the in vitro efficacy of chemotherapeutic drugs in multidrug resistant cancer cells.
the ability of nanomedicnes to overcome cellular multidrugs resistance is rather limited.

the development and characterization of novel nanomedicines for cancer treatment, with a particular focus on the ability of nanomedicinesto overcome cellular multidrugresistance (MDR) in cancer cells.
the development and application of novel nanomedicines.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the ability to overcome MDR is not a property of nanomedicnes as such, but of the individual nanomedicine formulation, and that this ability is not a prerequisite for the in vivo efficacy of a nanomedicine.
the classical nanomedicine strategies do not seem to be able to provide a major breakthrough for overcoming cellular MDR.
the ability of nanocarriers to overcome cellular M DR is highly dependent on the nature of the nanomedicine and the nature of the cancer cell line.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
nanomedicines do not seem to be able to overcome MDR in a significant way, but that they do have the ability to overcome the 'classical' pharmacological limitations of low-molecular weight drugs.
the use of nanocarriers to overcome cellular M.D.R. should be limited to the use of 'pharmacologically-active' nanomedicines only.

the use of nanomedicnes for overcoming cellular MDR may be justified in a limited number of cases, but that in most cases, alternative strategies, such as the use of P-glycoprotein inhibitors, may be more appropriate.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the cellular MDR phenotype should not be ignored when designing new nanomedicines.
